title: Business development manager salary: from hourly rates to annual pay
description: Learn how to convert a business development manager salary from hourly rates to annual figures under the Commercial Sales Award, including tax and super.
salarySummary: The minimum hourly rate for a business development manager under the Commercial Sales Award is $29.55 per hour, which equates to $58,390.80 per year for a 38-hour week before super and tax.

faqs.q: What is the minimum hourly rate for a business development manager in Australia?
faqs.a: Under the Commercial Sales Award (MA000083), the classification of commercial traveller has a minimum hourly rate of $29.55 as of 1 July 2026. This is the award floor for a business development manager who sells away from the employer's premises. Casual employees receive an additional 25% loading, making it $36.94 per hour.

faqs.q: How do I calculate the annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week (typically 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $29.55 × 38 × 52 = $58,390.80 per year. Superannuation of 12% is paid on top of this amount.

faqs.q: Does the award rate include superannuation?
faqs.a: No. The award rate is the minimum wage before super. Employers must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% (for 2026–27) on top of the ordinary time earnings. So the total cost to the employer is higher than the base salary.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the business development manager salary floor

When you’re looking at a **business development manager salary**, the first thing to know is that Australia has a system of minimum wages set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Most business development managers are covered by the Commercial Sales Award (MA000083), which sets a minimum hourly rate for the classification of commercial traveller. As of 1 July 2026, that rate is **$29.55 per hour** for a full-time adult employee.

This is the legal floor. It applies to employees who sell goods or services away from the employer’s premises – the classic field sales role. If the role is based in a shop or office, a different award may apply. The award also has a ladder of classifications: probationary traveller ($26.59), merchandiser ($27.47), commercial traveller ($29.55), and advertising sales representative ($29.55). The job title alone doesn’t decide the classification; it’s the work actually performed.

## How the hourly-to-annual conversion works

The standard formula we use on this site is straightforward: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For full-time work, we assume 38 hours per week, which is the ordinary hours under the National Employment Standards.

So for a business development manager on the award minimum:

$29.55 × 38 × 52 = **$58,390.80 per year**

That’s the gross annual wage before any additions. If you’re paid fortnightly, you can work it out as weekly pay × 2. Weekly pay is $29.55 × 38 = $1,122.90, so a fortnight is $2,245.80.

This formula assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. It’s a clean conversion for ordinary time earnings.

## What the Commercial Sales Award says

The award sets minimum rates, but it also includes allowances. For a business development manager who uses their own vehicle, the award specifies a rate per kilometre that must be paid on top of the hourly rate. Commission is separate – the award minimum is the base, and commission is a matter for the contract.

Casual employees get a 25% loading on top of the base rate. So a casual business development manager on the commercial traveller rate would earn $29.55 × 1.25 = **$36.94 per hour**. That loading is meant to compensate for not receiving paid leave like annual leave or sick leave.

It’s important to check the [pay guides](/blog) for the exact award that applies to your role. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for every award, and they include all monetary allowances and the most frequently used penalty rates.

## Tax and super: what comes on top

Your gross annual salary is not what you take home. Tax and the Medicare levy are deducted, and superannuation is paid on top by your employer.

For the 2026–27 income year, the resident tax rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners).

On a $58,390.80 salary, the tax would be roughly:
- $0 on first $18,200
- 15% on $26,800 ($45,000 – $18,200) = $4,020
- 30% on $13,390.80 ($58,390.80 – $45,000) = $4,017.24
- Total tax = $8,037.24
- Medicare levy 2% = $1,167.82
- Total deductions = $9,205.06
- Take-home pay ≈ $49,185.74 per year, or about $945.88 per week.

Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool for a more precise estimate.

Superannuation is separate. The super guarantee for 2026–27 is **12% of ordinary time earnings**, paid on top of your salary. So your employer’s total cost for a business development manager on the award floor is:

$58,390.80 (wages) + $7,006.90 (12% super) = **$65,397.70**

But super only applies up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830, so for most business development managers it’s a straight 12% on top. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

## The difference between award minimums and market rates

The award floor is the legal minimum, not the market rate. Many business development managers are paid above the award. The alisthiring.com analysis shows that the real cost to an employer at the award floor is about $67,504 when you include annual leave loading (17.5% of four weeks), super, and workers compensation. That’s roughly 15.6% on top of the wage.

But market rates can be significantly higher. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70 in May 2026, which equates to about $108,352 per year. A business development manager with experience might expect to be in that range, especially if commission is included.

When you’re negotiating a **business development manager salary**, remember that the award minimum is a starting point. The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) calculator on this site lets you enter any hourly rate to see the annual equivalent, the fortnightly pay, and the estimated tax and super.

Always check the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman to confirm the correct award and classification for your role. And if you’re a casual, remember to add the 25% loading before you do the conversion – never enter a rate that already includes casual loading into the calculator.

The formula is simple, but the context matters. Whether you’re an employer budgeting for a new hire or an employee comparing offers, understanding the full picture – award rates, super, tax, and market benchmarks – gives you a solid foundation.
